Colorado River Basin Idea Factory 2026

The Problem

Rural utilities are running on
institutional knowledge alone.

America's 45,000+ small water and wastewater utilities are the invisible backbone of public health. Most are staffed by one to three people managing complex treatment systems with decades-old equipment, minimal IT support, and no data intelligence layer. When something breaks, the fix lives in someone's head — or it doesn't exist at all.

With 1 in 3 experienced operators nearing retirement, that institutional knowledge is walking out the door — and there's no system in place to capture it before it's gone.

45K
small utilities across the U.S. — most without a data intelligence layer of any kind
🟢

Equipment That Outlives Its Documentation

Valves, pumps, and systems from the 1970s are still in daily operation. O&M manuals are lost, incomplete, or written for operators who retired long ago.

⚠️

Failures Escalate Before Anyone Notices

Without predictive monitoring, a slowly failing valve becomes a full-facility crisis. Influent keeps flowing while staff scramble — raising costs and straining already small teams.

📋

No Unified View of the System

SCADA data, paper logs, and institutional knowledge exist in silos. No single operator can see the full picture of their facility's health at a glance.

🧠

Expertise Has No Succession Plan

When the veteran operator retires — or has to leave the mountain — the knowledge that kept the system running goes with them. There's no playbook. No memory. No backup.

The Hidden Cost

$40K+

Wasted every year on over-dosed chemicals at a typical small utility — because operators are guessing without real-time feedback.

"When in doubt, pour it out." Without real-time process intelligence, operators add more chlorine, more coagulant, more polymer — just to feel safe. It's expensive, and it creates its own compliance risks.
30–50%
Chlorine Over-DosedExcess residual from manual guesswork

Creates disinfection byproducts (DBPs) — a compliance risk in their own right — and taste complaints from residents who notice the difference in their tap water.

20–40%
Coagulant & Polymer WasteDosed without real-time turbidity feedback

Chemical pumps are set conservatively high and left alone. No one watches the turbidity response in real time. Waste compounds every single day, invisibly.

Closes the LoopSensor data → AI recommendation → right dose

Real-time process feedback means operators dose with confidence, not anxiety. Less chemical. Better water. Typically $3,000–$6,000/year saved per facility.

The Platform

One smart brain for the whole system.

Upstream AI watches your wastewater & water facility around the clock, scores every reading for reliability, and tells operators what needs attention — before it becomes a crisis.

01

Unified System Overview

WTP and WWTP in one dashboard. Every metric, every alert — in plain language. Not fifty sensor screens.

02

Data Trust Engine

Every reading gets a confidence score. Chlorine at Trust 38%? Don't dose from that probe. Operators know what to believe before acting.

03

Predictive Alerts — Before Failures

Intelligent early warnings identify degrading equipment and process drift weeks before a valve fails, a pump seizes, or an alarm sounds at 2am.

04

Institutional Knowledge Vault

Captures operator expertise, process adjustments, and facility history. When the veteran retires, their knowledge stays in the system.

05

Mobile-First Design

Full plant status in under 10 seconds — from the truck, from home, from anywhere. Designed for operators, not engineers.

Core Feature — Morning Briefing

Before the operator arrives,
the AI has already been watching all night.

Overnight Summary — Automatic

Flow spikes, sensor anomalies, auto-adjustments — all summarized in plain language. No manual log review. The AI watched so the operator could sleep.

Your 3 Items Today — Prioritized

Not 400 alarms. Three specific, ranked tasks: check aeration diffusers, pull settleability test, calibrate chlorine probe. The operator knows exactly where to start.
